summary: Year 2 learners (ages 6-7) learn the key time-unit facts — 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day — and apply them in simple duration problems. Recall of the facts is usually secure; the real conceptual work is grasping the non-decimal 60-grouping (time is not base-10) and that a whole day is two 12-hour sweeps of the clock (24, not 12). The core approach is to count minutes in fives so a full 60 closes into one hour, and to track the hour hand's double sweep across day and night.
misconceptions: Thinks a day is 12 hours because the clock face 'stops at 12'
Over-applies base-10 — treats 1 hour as 100 minutes, 90 minutes as 9 hours, or half an hour as 50 minutes
Fails to regroup at 60 when adding times (3:40 + 30 minutes = 3:70)
Muddles which unit is larger (minute vs hour)

activities.title: The hour hand's double lap: why a day is 24 hours
steps: Move the hour hand slowly round an analogue clock from midday, naming the hours aloud as it passes the numbers.
When the hand returns to 12, pause and count: that first lap covered 12 hours (midday through to midnight).
Send the hand round a second time, now naming the night and morning hours, and track a day-strip that fills behind the clock — one half for the first lap, the second half for the second lap.
Write down the total: 12 + 12 = 24 hours in a whole day and night.
Line a 12-hour clock up beside a 24-hour clock so that, for example, 1pm matches 13:00, confirming the numbers 1-12 get used twice.
activities.insight: A whole day is 24 hours because the hour hand goes round the 12-number clock face twice — once from midday to midnight and once from midnight to midday — so 12 + 12 = 24, not 12. One lap alone is 12 hours; it takes two laps to make a day.

activities.title: Closing the hour at 60: the non-decimal grouping
steps: Count minutes in fives around a clock face or along a number line marked in minutes, saying 5, 10, 15 … up to 60.
Notice that it takes exactly 60 minutes for the minute hand to complete one full lap (twelve jumps of 5), so 60 minutes close into 1 hour.
Contrast this with money/base-10 out loud: an hour is 60 minutes, NOT 100 — time does not group in tens and hundreds.
Fill an 'hour container' that only closes at 60: pour in 90 minutes and watch it overflow into one full hour (60) with 30 left over.
Record the result: 90 minutes = 1 hour 30 minutes, because 90 = 60 + 30.
activities.insight: Minutes regroup into hours at 60, not at 100: a full 60 minutes makes one hour, so 90 minutes is 1 hour 30 minutes — the grouping is felt by counting and overflowing, not just recited.

activities.title: Apply the facts: simple duration problems
steps: Solve a duration problem such as: 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?' and state the answer as 1 hour 30 minutes.
Answer a day question with reasoning: 'How many hours are in one whole day and night, and why — when the clock only shows 1 to 12?'
Decide which unit is larger, a minute or an hour, and justify it.
Explain each answer in words, not just give the number, so the reasoning is visible.
activities.insight: The time-unit facts are tools to be used: a learner who understands them can convert 90 minutes to 1 hour 30 and explain 24 hours as two 12-hour sweeps, transferring the reasoning to fresh problems.

checkQuestion: Ask the fact, then the reason. (A) 'How many hours are there in one whole day and night? ... The clock face only shows the numbers 1 to 12 — so how can a day have that many hours? Tell me why.' (B) 'A cartoon lasts 90 minutes. How many hours and minutes is that, and how do you know?'
checkAnswer: (A) 24 hours, because the hour hand goes round the clock twice — 12 hours through the morning and 12 more through the afternoon and night, so 12 + 12 = 24. (B) 1 hour 30 minutes, because 60 minutes make one hour and 90 = 60 + 30.
